column2: The open saddlebags and arrows give you more to examine than the bodies alone. Beyond the bend, trunks and tangled growth break up the view into the woods; anyone moving closer will have to choose where to stand and what to watch.

Each disturbed patch offers a place to slow down and look, while the thicker growth limits what you can see ahead. You can keep the heavier marks in view, check the ground before committing your weight, or pause to decide how closely you want to follow.

The stream and the strip of dry ground offer different approaches to the same black opening. From outside, you can study the banks and the briars before stepping beneath the hill; the sound of running water makes the darkness beyond seem deeper.

The vegetation interrupts your view of whatever lies beyond it. The stream remains an obvious landmark beside the approach, but the brief creak gives you a reason to watch the cover rather than hurry past it.

The scrape of the chains marks the animals' movements more clearly than the dim light does. There is little room to spread out here, and the growling rises when attention turns toward them. You can stop at the edge of the chamber before choosing how to approach.

Water follows the slope past your boots, leaving the rising stone slick and dark. The crossing overhead is separate from the route at your feet; from here, you can judge the climb and look for movement above without knowing where either passage ends.

The bridge's boards and supports stand out against the rock when your light catches them. Below, the stream continues along the climbing passage. The figure above and the louder water ahead give you two different things to watch as you decide whether to advance.

The ordinary sounds of the cave return around the fading sensation: dripping stone, your breathing, and the stream finding its channel again. Nothing in that brief feeling identifies a source. You have a moment to check one another and decide whether to mention what you noticed.

The rough barriers hold back a great deal of water, and the noise fills the space around them. You can inspect their visible supports, look for ground that stays out of the current, or study the onward route before putting someone beside a dam.

The stacked goods divide the cavern into patches of cover and narrow sightlines. Firelight catches the raised weapon and the wolf's teeth, while smoke drifts toward the opening overhead. The way you entered remains behind you as you choose how to answer this reception.

The passage is still close enough that a voice raised here could carry farther than intended. Sildar's words give you a name and an object to ask about, but not a destination. There is time to hear him out, check what help he needs, and decide where to take the conversation.

Your equipment and companions are the immediate things within reach; the rest of the journey will depend on what you choose to do with them. You can make room for someone who needs help, compare the leads you actually found, or take a moment to prepare before moving on.

The trading house offers an obvious place to ask questions or settle the delivery, while the street leaves you free to keep walking. Its traffic is ordinary enough that you can watch the doorway, approach together, or decide who will speak before going inside.

The shelves are arranged for practical journeys rather than impressive purchases: coils of rope, provisions, and tools ready to be carried away. The counter is a place to set down goods or ask for help, and the shopkeeper waits to hear which business brought you through his door.

The street gives him several places to begin an inquiry, but his glance does not settle on an answer. Shops, passing residents, and the possibility of a shared meeting place lie within reach. You can accompany him or agree where to find one another after making your own inquiries.

Tables and travel-worn clothing break up the room, leaving conversations close enough to approach without addressing everyone at once. The child's sudden quiet is one detail among several. You can choose a seat, seek the keeper, or listen before deciding whose story you want to hear.

Their attention gives the encounter an immediate edge, but the street still offers space to speak or withdraw. Before anyone reaches for a weapon, you can look at where the strangers stand and decide whether to answer together, keep your distance, or let one person do the talking.

The cistern and the stored goods make this a working space rather than a grand entrance. Watch where the floor leaves room to move between them. You can examine the water, check the visible doors, or establish a position before continuing farther below the manor.

The bedding and personal clutter suggest repeated use rather than a room abandoned with the house above. The space between the sleeping places is worth noting before you enter. You can look over what is plainly visible or watch the exit while someone examines the room.

The hall gives you a direct way forward, but its floor deserves as much attention as its far end. Dust, joins in the stone, and the places where boots might fall are visible things to inspect. You can slow the group or check the route without assuming that the way is safe.

The stonework muffles the noise from elsewhere in the hideout, making a small movement feel unusually loud. The resting places and scattered remains offer different things to examine. You can leave them undisturbed, look for names or damage, or keep watch while another person searches.

The bars turn the room into a place of confinement rather than ordinary storage. The doors and the space beside them matter if anyone is to leave in a hurry. You can address whoever is actually present, inspect the locks, or check the surrounding route before promising a way out.

The arrangement of the stored equipment makes it possible to examine one part of the room without disturbing everything else. You can check what is within reach, look for markings, or study the exits. Anything useful still has to be inspected before you decide to carry it away.

The break in the cavern floor divides your approach into separate stretches of ground. Its edges and any visible crossing deserve a careful look before someone moves ahead. You can stop to judge the drop or keep to the near side while deciding what you want to investigate.

The room's sleeping places and the positions of those inside shape the space available for an approach. You have a moment to note who watches you, who avoids your gaze, and where the door sits behind you. Words are still an option before the first movement becomes an attack.

The tables and scattered possessions make this a room people spend time in, not simply a passage to somewhere else. You can take in the faces and the gaps between the furniture before answering. Whether you listen, bluff, or confront them, their reactions are something you can actually observe.

The worktable, shelves, and unfamiliar apparatus offer several separate lines of inquiry. You can examine the written material without assuming what the equipment does, or look over the apparatus without touching it. The ordinary routes through the room remain worth keeping clear while you investigate.

The desk and chest suggest different sorts of business: work done in the open and possessions kept close. You can examine what is visible, listen toward the adjoining spaces, or check the way you came. Nothing here tells you what happened after someone left without further evidence.

The shop doorway is close at hand, while the inn and the rest of town remain separate places to visit. You can settle ordinary business first, check on the companion you left behind, or give Trista room to decide what to do with her captive. The next step belongs to you.

The change in the ground and the narrowing view make it worth agreeing who leads and how closely you follow. Grass gives way to cover where the trail bends, and the last clear stretch of road is now behind you. You can pause to check your bearings before taking the next turn.

The low shelter makes a close approach very different from calling out at a distance. Still branches frame the entrance, and the voice waits for an answer. You can offer your purpose plainly, choose your words with care, or keep to the edge of the clearing while you speak.

The broken stone is a landmark you can recognize without deciding what happened after your departure. You can compare the ground and the tower with your last visit, look for an actual new trace, or keep watch while someone examines the place more closely.

The familiar approach gives you a point from which to compare what is here now with what you remember. The ravine and the opening remain useful landmarks. You can look for a specific change, approach the cave cautiously, or leave the cleared camp behind without searching it again.

The warning and the tower give you landmarks before you commit to any particular building. Between the ruined walls, the growth interrupts sightlines and makes some paths clearer than others. You can read the sign, study the nearest approach, or decide how to keep your companions in view.

The broken upper stonework does not make the lower walls transparent. Trees still provide places to stop and observe, while the rise exposes anyone who crosses it. You can count visible approaches, watch the slit for another movement, or withdraw to discuss a quieter route.

The wrecked timbers interrupt a straight walk through the entrance. The narrow openings above offer views into the approach without giving you the same view back. You can study the wall from cover, look for a clearer way through, or decide who will cross the exposed ground first.

The fallen plaster marks one part of the floor as different from the rest. Beyond it, the closed doors give you choices without revealing what lies behind them. You can inspect the ground, listen at a door, or choose a position that keeps the entrance in sight.

The cleared strip and the bedding are more recent signs than the fallen masonry around them. You can follow the space someone has made through the rubble or stop to examine how it is being used. The damaged tower offers no assurance that everyone inside is asleep or absent.

The recognizable equipment is within a room still crowded by old stores. You can examine its markings and condition without deciding how it came here. The casks and provisions break up the floor around it, so someone can watch the entrance while another person investigates.

The swept floor and arranged weapons stand out against the ruin you passed on the way here. The pallets leave recognizable places to rest and narrow spaces to move between them. You can inspect the room from its edge or check which visible exit you want watched.

The two tables take up much of the social space, with the neglected brazier drawing stale smells around it. The voices give you something to listen to before you answer them. You can remain at the edge, make your presence clear, or take stock of the route back out.

The carvings reward a closer look, but the curtains prevent you from seeing the spaces beyond them. The stone brazier is a visible landmark between those covered openings. You can study the workmanship, listen toward the cloth, or decide whether to move farther into the hall.

The cloth hides much of the altar's surface, while the implements catch what light reaches the room. The watchers' attention rests on the curtains as well as on you. You can address them from where you stand, inspect what is visible, or withdraw before disturbing the arrangement.

The door offers a more contained approach than the wrecked main entrance, but the slits still overlook the ground before it. Brush crowds the path around your feet. You can examine the door and wall from a distance or decide how to approach without assuming the entrance is unwatched.

The canvas and vegetation break up the outline of what the tower used to be. The crates are the clearest remaining sign of its practical use. You can examine a visible patch of ground, check beneath accessible cover, or keep the ruined approach in sight while someone searches.

The brazier's glow reaches the pallets more readily than it reaches beyond the hanging cloth. The curtain separates what you can see from what you can only hear. You can pause to listen, examine the guardroom, or decide who will stand nearest the covered arch.

The barred door gives you a boundary you can choose to keep. The weight behind it is audible before it is visible, and the wood's movement gives you reason to judge your distance. You can listen, examine the fastening, or leave the barrier intact while discussing another route.

The argument reveals different voices, not an agreement you understand yet. The furs and the speakers' positions divide the room into places to approach or avoid. You can listen for a few more words, announce yourselves, or look for a position that keeps your way out clear.

The approaching sounds give you time to look toward cover and the route you used to reach the castle. How clearly you can see the patrol depends on where you stand. You can wait to learn more, call out, or decide whether to leave before the meeting becomes unavoidable.

The opening offers a visible threshold, but the sound beyond it reaches farther than your sight. The rocky approach gives you a place to check equipment and gather your light before entering. You can study the ground, agree on your order, or listen for the next distant surge.

The rope is the clearest connection between this camp and the space below. Its fastening and the edge of the pit can be examined before anyone descends. The bundles and the body offer separate questions, and you can leave room for someone to keep watch while the others decide where to begin.

The low stonework makes every turn feel close, and the unfinished faces give several branches a similar appearance. You can keep a mark at the last junction, follow the group carefully, or stop to compare the visible passages before choosing one. Your route back is something you can record as you go.

The abandoned lamps offer no light of their own. Your illumination catches the miners' carved tools and the pale bones at different heights, leaving the upper space harder to judge. You can inspect the floor, examine the figures on the walls, or direct your attention toward the ceiling.

The bunks identify this as a place where people once slept, while the broken racks suggest equipment no longer fit for use. Fallen stone interrupts parts of the floor. You can study the room from the threshold, choose a route through the debris, or examine a particular set of remains.

The arrangement of the scales and niches suggests work that once involved careful measurements and records. The scraps are within reach, but their age is visible in their edges. You can look without touching, search the counter, or ask someone who knows the writing to examine what survives.

The bunks and old brazier break the chamber into narrower gaps than its size first suggests. The shapes among the bones are occupied with what lies before them. You can stop at the entrance to judge those gaps, choose where to stand, or decide whether to make your presence known.

The half-open door breaks the line of the collapsed wall. Beyond it, cracked kegs still stand in something like their old order, a small island of storage amid the ruin. The sound of stonework carries here; its source remains out of sight.

The faint green light clings to the caps and stalks, leaving the room's edges hard to judge. The growth covers the walking surface as well as the view ahead. Before crossing, you can study its spread from the threshold and decide how close to bring your light.

Cold braziers offer no warmth to the long tables. The stairs and ledges at either end rise above the scattered remains, giving the chamber more than one level to watch. Anything moving across the open floor would be difficult to overlook from above.

The bank's shells crunch beneath a careful step, while the black water gives little sense of its depth. The stream's low northeastern opening draws your eye away from the pool. Following it would mean approaching stone and water that conceal what lies beyond.

The brazier's warmth sets this room apart from the colder passages. Bunks leave narrow spaces between them, and the broken table piled against the eastern door makes that exit a practical obstacle. You can inspect the barricade from this side before deciding whether to disturb it.

Ore carts stand idle beside the furnace, and the wheel hangs motionless over a dry channel. Green fire outlines the skull and catches on the armored dead. The old machinery divides the floor into working spaces; the threat now occupies the same ground where miners once labored.

Points of light prick the ceiling above the two blackened buildings. Down below, fallen bodies and scorched stone tell a harsher story. The buildings interrupt the open cavern, each offering a closer approach and a separate interior to examine.

Charred furniture crowds the room beneath the damaged ceiling. The bed and chest survived the destruction well enough to recognize, though their contents cannot be judged from here. The dark presence near the floor draws attention away from them, making the threshold a useful place to stop and look.

The brazier's green light colors the scorched tables, while the many-eyed creature hangs within the ruined workspace. Its greeting reaches you without crossing the air. There is room to answer before moving closer; the surviving forge equipment remains something to study rather than claim on sight.

Each surge changes the sound of the cavern, filling the spaces between words before falling away again. The water and the stone around it are visible things to study. You can keep back from its edge, watch the rhythm, or inspect the route without entering the water.

Smooth stones lie among larger boulders in the dry channel. With the ceiling hanging low, the route asks you to watch both your footing and your head. Its bends and obstructions break the view ahead; you can keep track of the way back as you pass them.

The waterfall fills the rift with a steady roar, broken by the clacking work below. Ropes fastened to stakes on the western side offer a visible means of descent. From the edge, you can examine their condition and the figures beneath before committing to the drop.

The figures and stonework draw your eye to different parts of the room. You can note where everyone stands and which route remains behind you before answering. The distance between you and anyone present is something to consider while there is still time to speak.

The words being exchanged do not settle what either side will accept. You can hold your position, ask for a specific answer, or make your own terms clear. The chamber and the route behind you remain part of the conversation, even if nobody chooses to mention them.

You can take stock from the threshold before approaching what lies within. The visible condition of any person here and the space around them matter more than guessing what happened out of sight. You can offer help, ask a question, or check the way out before moving someone.

The places you recognize offer somewhere to begin your account, but the people who hear it will need your words. You can tell them what you witnessed, ask what changed during your absence, or settle a practical need before deciding what comes after the expedition.

The cell's closed door places a boundary between the prisoner and everyone outside. Questions can wait long enough to decide who stands watch and who speaks. Whatever answer Nezznar offers will still need to be weighed against what you have actually seen.

The shop's threshold is close enough to cross, but you have not yet chosen to enter. You can begin with town business, turn back toward the inn, or stop to discuss the rat in Trista's care. For now, the street leaves each of those choices open.

The counter offers room to set down goods or explain what brought you here. Barthen waits for your account rather than supplying one of his own. You can ask for ordinary equipment, discuss the supplies, or tell him only as much of your recent trouble as you choose.

The place you left him is the first thing to check, before any questions about the wider trouble. You can ask the keeper to take you there, find out who has been nearby, or arrange for someone to watch the approach. Gundren's present condition is something you must see for yourselves.

The rat's containment is something you can check before beginning an examination. What you know so far comes from the capture, not from any explanation it has given you. You can observe it, ask Trista what help she wants, or leave the question for another meeting.

The manor is a landmark, not an account of what remains inside it. People who were actually present may have different parts of the story. You can choose a particular witness, return along a known approach, or turn toward another town matter without settling the gang's future here and now.

The well above is a visible link to the world you left, while the sand records each new step beneath it. The shields offer battered surfaces to examine along the walls. You can check the landing, study the passage, or look back up before leaving the chamber.

The pillars interrupt a clear view across the room, and the shallow steps mark a change in the floor beneath you. Your light follows the demon carvings more easily than it follows the spaces between the columns. You can stop at the descent and choose what to watch.

The slope carries the foul water toward deeper parts of the floor. The violet light makes the damaged figure visible without explaining what the statue was meant to do. You can study it from the shallower ground or look for a practical route around the water.

The sword and its support stand apart from the small remains on the floor. Above, the vents carry sound from a space you cannot see. You can listen without touching the weapon, inspect the bones, or examine how the wooden support holds the blade.

The bones have been worked into the pillars themselves, while other remains lie loose below them. The alcoves give your light several dark recesses to reach into. You can inspect one opening at a time or keep to a position where you can watch the room around you.

The stone figures have outlasted the broken objects at their feet. Their fixed expressions contrast with the living sound from the adjoining spaces. You can listen before approaching that light, inspect the damaged staff, or decide how plainly to announce yourselves.

The frescoes repeat their frightened movement even where age has worn away the color. Bedding lies beneath the painted scene, leaving old decoration and more practical use side by side. You can examine the art, check the abandoned resting places, or continue along the passage.

The high seat draws your eye upward, but the crystal fragments and remains make the floor worth watching as well. Lantern light reaches from the nearby rooms without showing everything inside them. You can inspect the debris or pause to listen before following the glow.

The empty sockets in the pillars offer a pattern to examine separately from the body on the floor. Discarded weapons lie close enough to suggest questions, not answers. You can check the remains, study the stripped stonework, or watch the room while someone searches.

The skulls roll and knock against one another before settling among the dust. The doorway is now partly crowded by what fell through it. You can keep back while the movement stops, examine the exposed threshold, or look into the space the door has opened.

The copper catches the light through the film of age, giving the throne and helm a muted green sheen. Cobwebs connect details that may once have mattered to whoever used the seat. You can inspect the workmanship or judge the surrounding floor before approaching the throne.

The statues form repeated shapes beneath the hanging webs, and the bolts make the dead spiders more than a passing detail. You can look for a clear way between the figures, examine the visible missiles, or keep your light directed toward the ceiling.

The end wall gives this room a clear boundary, and the passage you entered remains the obvious way back. There is no grand furnishing to draw your eye away from the stone itself. You can examine its surfaces or leave it as a useful landmark on your route.

The suspended water is above the statue rather than resting in a basin at its feet. The box and the figure's four arms give you specific parts to examine. You can remain in the passage, study the arrangement, or choose a closer position without touching it.

The fallen racks interrupt the floor on the way to the door. The handaxe marks a particular place in the wood that you can inspect before opening anything. You can look over the surrounding debris or listen beyond the barrier before deciding what to try.

The nests are built from things that once belonged elsewhere: cloth, broken stone, and bones brought together in heaps. Their size is easier to judge than their owners' whereabouts. You can examine an edge from a distance or keep clear of the piles while checking the chamber.

The figures have poses that invite a closer look, while the dark statue catches light differently from the rest. The dead reptile is another visible detail to examine rather than an explanation for the whole room. You can study the scene without stepping among the figures.

The smell reaches you before a clear view of the chamber does. The nearer floor and the mouth of the room offer places to stop and look. You can listen, inspect the approach, or decide whether to announce your presence before entering the filth.

The tables and rods suggest old work, but their present emptiness leaves its purpose for you to investigate. You can follow the arrangement of the stone furniture, look for marks where things once hung, or keep to the open floor while checking the adjoining halls.

The iron face turns an ordinary-looking barrier into something worth examining. Its smile does not show what waits on the other side. You can inspect the visible fittings, speak from a distance, or listen at the door before deciding whether to try it.

The mirrors repeat the corridor and the light you bring into it, making the walls seem less solid than the floor beneath your boots. The spent torch is a small, tangible detail amid those reflections. You can inspect a surface or study the ground without trusting every image equally.

The spent torches and empty bottles show that someone stopped here, but not that they will return. You can examine the traces, note the approach, or discuss whether this is a place worth checking more carefully. A recognizable resting place is not a promise of safety.

The voices give the connected rooms a sense of occupation before you can see everyone inside them. You can stop to listen for words, decide whether to call out, or take a position that leaves the route behind you clear. The conversation need not begin with a drawn weapon.

The arch and the chained remains give you two distinct things to examine. Old bones lie loose near one feature and held in place near the other. You can study the surrounding stonework, inspect a fastening, or keep your distance while comparing what you see.

The tools remain at the mouth of work that changes from built stone to a rough opening through rubble. The low clearance is visible before you enter. You can check the unstable-looking ground, judge what equipment will fit, or leave a mark identifying the way back.

The floating lights make the lack of dust especially noticeable. You can compare this floor with the passages you have already crossed, watch a candle without reaching for it, or inspect the corridor one section at a time. The difference is visible; its cause is not yet established.

The carved musician and the broken pole share the space without explaining one another. Your light follows the relief's edges and the jagged break in the wood. You can examine either object, listen in the chamber, or keep the visible approach watched while someone takes notes.

The bedding shows everyday use around a monument whose carved eye is harder to ignore. The frightened voices come from beyond what you can plainly see. You can answer them, inspect the obelisk from a distance, or look for a position that allows the speakers room to approach.

The shields line the way toward the hovering shape, giving you landmarks between yourself and it. The eye is visible, but its intention is not. You can stop, speak, study what it does, or keep the passage behind you available while choosing your next move.

The draft carries sound around the turn, but the bend keeps the far stretch out of view. You can judge the doorway and the nearer floor before committing to the passage. The wind gives you something to listen to as well as something to push against.

The grooves and shifted base make one part of the floor different from the rest. The statues stand in their alcoves while those marks cross the ground before them. You can follow the visible traces, inspect a plinth, or leave someone watching the hall.

The carved walls imitate natural stone closely enough to reward a second look. Tool-work and rock are part of the same view here. You can compare the surfaces, look for where one carved feature meets another, or follow the visible passage without disturbing anything.

The bare shelves offer places where sleepers once lay, but little personal clutter remains to tell you who they were. You can examine a particular recess or study the floor between them. The repeated stone shapes also give you a way to describe this room on your map.

The webbing connects the remains to the bed beneath them, making the untouched areas worth distinguishing from the paths between the stone frames. You can look closely without reaching in, keep watch over the room, or choose to leave the resting place undisturbed.

The ajar door lets you listen before entering, while the ruined throne makes the sleeping rat easy to place within the room. You can keep your distance, inspect the visible floor, or consider how much noise an approach would make. The animal has not yet answered your presence.

The broken figures and fallen stone complicate a quick approach to the closed door. The weeping gives you a direction without a clear view of its source. You can call through the barrier, inspect the nearer ground, or decide who will listen while the others watch the hall.

The wall drawing gives you something enormous to study, while the pit demands attention to where you put your feet. Movement below is only partly visible from its edge. You can remain back, examine the cutaway, or choose a careful place from which to look down.

The prints offer a trail to inspect rather than a person already in view. The curve hides the next stretch of passage, leaving the near dust as your clearest evidence. You can compare the marks, listen around the bend, or record where you first saw them.

The king's two faces look over the same chamber while the quarrel reaches you from the north. The column interrupts part of that view. You can study the stone figure, listen for the speakers' words, or decide where to stand before drawing their attention.

The spears make a repeated pattern until the gleaming weapon breaks it. The statues' height lets you study some details more easily than others. You can compare the three figures from the floor, inspect the surrounding space, or decide how closely to approach the unusual spear.

The fissure gives your light a dark line to follow overhead, while the wheelbarrows keep the room's former work close at hand. You can inspect the debris, examine a tool, or look up before crossing beneath the damaged ceiling. The room offers questions at more than one height.

The press of the streets gives you practical choices immediately: where to keep together, where to stop, and whom to ask for directions. Bells and calls overlap above the rolling carts. There is time to choose your first destination rather than let the crowd choose it for you.

The offered seats give the conversation somewhere to begin without turning it into a formal report. You can set down what you choose to share and keep the rest close. Dracuseth waits for your account, leaving the first questions and the pace of the meeting to you.

The well draws a circle of attention through the room, with ordinary conversation continuing around it. The creak of the rope gives you a reminder of the space below. You can find a table, ask about the descent, or watch how others approach the opening.

The separate trays give every page a place without requiring you to settle its meaning first. You can offer an observation, ask how it could be checked, or keep a detail private. The clean sheet leaves room to write down a question before anyone chooses an answer.

The dishes and instruments are within sight, but the tool is presented for your inspection rather than pressed into use. You can ask what each part does and which test it permits. Your belongings remain yours to keep untouched until you agree otherwise.

The folded paper offers a proposal you can inspect without committing to it. You can read the request, ask who delivered it, or leave it beside the cup for later. A meeting can be accepted, postponed, or refused before any wider obligation is discussed.

The rope and the route sheet suggest two different sorts of preparation: what will help you descend and what will help someone understand your return. You can discuss a stopping point, check the equipment, or ask what information is expected before taking the first step.

The familiar entrance offers a place to pause before your account becomes someone else's retelling. You can decide what to carry inside, what needs care, and what should be recorded first. The city's ordinary noise continues around the discoveries you brought back.

The weeds interrupt a straight approach to the doorway, and the open roof leaves the cottage exposed to the sky. You can examine the nearer ground, look through the ruined walls, or keep watch beneath the broad tree before choosing how to enter.

The brush has grown across what used to separate the homes' rooms. Fallen walls still mark their old boundaries beneath the living growth. You can inspect a particular patch of rubble or keep together where the route between the two ruins is easiest to see.

The hanging sign gives the ruin a name even though its hospitality is long gone. The slumped forms are visible among the remains of ordinary tavern furnishings. You can stop at the doorway to study them, call into the room, or decide where to stand before entering.

The cleared approach and sturdy shutters set this house apart from its neighbors. They give you somewhere to knock or call without pushing through the overgrowth. You can announce yourselves, inspect the outside, or wait at a respectful distance for someone to answer.

The tangle of shrubs hides parts of the ground where the walls once stood. The movement in the leaves is brief enough to invite attention rather than an immediate explanation. You can stop disturbing the stones, look for a clearer position, or watch the growth while discussing the approach.

The strands cross the lane as well as the building, making the approach itself worth examining. Your light catches some threads more readily than the shadows behind them. You can study the webbing from clear ground or decide how much of the lane you want to cross.

The dead spiders give the tower's sharp smell a more tangible companion. Broken stone and the open upper roof offer places to look before you approach the entrance. You can keep your distance, seek another view of the structure, or pause to decide what danger you are willing to meet.

The chimney remains a landmark above the rotten construction, while the shapes inside sit among the traces of old work. You can watch them from the entrance, inspect the nearby ground, or listen before disturbing the room. The forge's former purpose does not explain its present occupants.

Glass fragments and damaged pages share the floor beneath the shelving. You can examine one storage place at a time rather than overturn the whole room. If someone has given you a description to follow, you can compare it with what you actually see here.

The warrior's pose remains visible despite the statue's lean, and the paths offer several different ways to leave the square. You can study the carving, check your bearings against the surrounding ruins, or choose the next approach with the whole group in sight.

The surviving roof makes the barracks feel more enclosed than the cottages outside. Narrow windows admit limited views, while beds and old armor divide the interior. You can stop to examine the threshold, look over the room, or listen before touching any of the remains.

The broken loom identifies one kind of work once done here. Beyond it, the southern growth conceals ground you cannot yet judge. You can examine the cottage's visible remains or keep back from the thicket while deciding where to direct your attention.

The voices make the barred shutters more than a sign of an abandoned house. They offer a chance to speak before attempting to get inside. You can call from the approach, listen for a response, or stand where the occupants can see you if they choose to look out.

The rectangle leaves most of the paper empty. Beside the cups, Ilvara's clean sheet offers room for turns, blocked passages, and the point where your light or courage ran short. She waits for your questions before the first route is agreed.

The sand gives you a surface on which to notice fresh tracks or leave a deliberate mark. The hanging shields frame the chamber, but the bend hides the next stretch. The circle overhead remains the clearest landmark for the way back.

The pillars divide sight into narrow lanes, and the steps change the height of the floor beneath your feet. The scratched warning is easy to read; whether it deserves belief is another matter. You can examine each visible exit before choosing one.

Old bones lie below the carved nobles, while the speaker's clothes and measured smile hold your attention. There is a demand on the table, but no agreement yet. The space between you leaves time to ask who collects this toll and what it buys.

The blank edge marks the boundary of what you have checked. Beyond it, a passage can be investigated or left honestly unfinished. You can compare the light and supplies still in hand with the route you already know before choosing to continue.

A turn that was unfamiliar on the descent now has a place in your account. Your marks give you something concrete to check as you retrace the route. The unanswered branches remain where you left them, without requiring an answer tonight.

The notch is small enough to overlook until Orren points it out. His drawing records a particular tool rather than a chest of interchangeable brass. You can ask what condition matters, what handling is permitted, and how he would recognize an altered instrument.

The notebook stays closed between the cups. Kestrel offers a conversation, not unrestricted access to her crew's work. You can name a route or question you would exchange before deciding whether either side should open its records.
